tool.name: SQLite
tool.tagline: Serverless SQL database engine stored in a single file
tool.description: SQLite is a small, fast, self-contained SQL database engine that runs inside your application and stores the whole database in one ordinary file. It is the most widely deployed database in the world, built into phones, browsers, desktop apps and Python's standard library. It is ideal for local and embedded storage, tests, data analysis and many single-server web apps.

glossary.def: A command for the sqlite3 tool that starts with a dot, such as .tables or .import. The tool handles it itself; it isn't SQL.
The type an SQLite value actually has: NULL, INTEGER, REAL, TEXT or BLOB. Each value carries its own, whatever the column says.
In SQLite, a column's preferred type, worked out from its declared type name. SQLite converts values towards it when it can, but doesn't reject those it can't.
The hidden whole-number key of every ordinary SQLite table. Rows are stored in rowid order, so looking one up by rowid is the fastest access.
An SQLite option on INTEGER PRIMARY KEY that guarantees an id is never handed out twice, even after the newest row is deleted.
An SQLite table created with the STRICT keyword (3.37+), which rejects values that don't fit a column's declared type.
An SQLite statement that reads or changes a setting, or inspects the database, e.g. PRAGMA foreign_keys = ON.
How long an SQLite connection waits for a lock held by someone else before giving up with 'database is locked'.
SQLite's 'database is locked' error: another connection holds the lock you need, and waiting didn't help or wasn't allowed.
SQLite's default way of making transactions safe: it copies the original pages to a side file before changing them, so a crash can be undone.
An SQLite journal mode in which changes are added to a separate -wal file first, so readers and the one writer don't block each other.
In SQLite's WAL mode, the step that copies changes from the -wal file back into the main database file.
In SQLite, a command that rebuilds the whole database file, leaving out unused pages so the file shrinks.
In SQLite, one fixed-size block of the database file (4096 bytes by default). Tables and indexes are made of pages.
SQLite's list of unused pages inside the database file, kept for reuse after rows are deleted.
An extra SQLite page holding the part of a row too big to fit in its normal page.
Changing an SQLite table that ALTER TABLE can't change: create a new table, copy the rows over, drop the old one and rename the new one.
A number stored in an SQLite file that you set and read with PRAGMA user_version, commonly used to record which schema changes have run.
In SQLite (3.45+), a compact binary form of JSON stored in a BLOB and handled by the jsonb_ functions; faster to process than JSON text.
SQLite's full-text search extension: a special table that indexes words so MATCH queries find and rank documents quickly.
An SQLite table whose rows are produced by code, such as FTS5, instead of being stored the ordinary way. You query it with normal SQL.
A standard formula for scoring how well a document matches a search, used by SQLite's FTS5 to rank results.
An FTS5 table that indexes the text of another, ordinary table instead of storing its own copy.
SQLite's Virtual Database Engine: the built-in interpreter that runs the bytecode SQLite compiles each statement into.
One instruction in a bytecode program, such as SQLite's OpenRead or ResultRow.
A store of already-compiled statements kept per connection, so running the same SQL text again skips compiling it.
SQLite's built-in way to copy a database that is in use into another file safely, e.g. con.backup() in Python.
A separate tool that continuously copies an SQLite database's changes to cloud storage, so it can be restored to a recent moment.
SQLite's built-in table listing every table, index, view and trigger with the SQL that created it.

concepts.name: What SQLite is and when to use it
concepts.summary: SQLite is a database that runs inside your app and keeps everything in one ordinary file, with no server to install.
concepts.why: Knowing how SQLite works tells you when it's the perfect choice and when you need a server database such as PostgreSQL or MySQL.
concepts.body:
Most databases run as a server: a separate program that your app sends SQL to, often over a network. **SQLite** is different. It is a small piece of ready-made code, a **library**, built into your app itself. Reading and writing the database is just your app running that code; nothing travels over a network.

There's nothing to install, set up or keep running. The whole database (tables, indexes, everything) lives in **one ordinary file** that you can copy, email or keep next to your tests.

It is still a real SQL database. Transactions are all-or-nothing and survive crashes and power cuts, and it supports joins, upserts (insert-or-update in one statement) and most advanced SQL features.

It is also the most widely used database in the world: it ships inside every phone, every major web browser and the Python programming language.

Great fits:

- Storing an app's data on the device: desktop, mobile and gadget apps.
- Tests, prototypes, small programs and data analysis.
- Websites and services that run on **one server** and mostly read data; many handle a lot of traffic.

Poor fits: many app servers writing to one database over a network (SQLite allows only **one writer at a time**, and shared network drives break the locks it relies on); very many simultaneous writes; or data so large it must be spread over several machines. Then choose PostgreSQL or MySQL.
takeaways: SQLite runs inside your app; the whole database is one file
It's a full SQL database whose transactions survive crashes
Great for local, embedded and single-server use; only one writer at a time
pitfalls: Putting a SQLite file on a shared network drive used by several computers.

quiz.q: Which situation is the weakest fit for SQLite?
options: Unit tests needing a throwaway database
Ten application servers writing concurrently to one database over the network
A read-heavy blog on one server
quiz.explain: SQLite allows one writer at a time and relies on file locks that shared network drives don't handle reliably.

concepts.name: The sqlite3 command-line shell
concepts.summary: Open a database with the sqlite3 command-line tool, run SQL, and use dot-commands to inspect tables and load or save data.
concepts.why: The sqlite3 tool is the fastest way to look inside a SQLite file, fix data or load a spreadsheet's data.
concepts.body:
`sqlite3` is a small program you run in a **terminal**: the text window where you type commands instead of clicking icons. `sqlite3 shop.db` opens that database file, creating it if needed; `sqlite3` alone opens a temporary database that disappears when you quit. Then type SQL statements ending with `;` after its **prompt**, `sqlite>`, which shows it is waiting for you.

Commands that start with a dot, **dot-commands**, are handled by the sqlite3 tool itself instead of being run as SQL:

- `.tables` lists tables; `.schema product` shows the `CREATE` statement for product.
- `.headers on` and `.mode box` (or `column`, `table`, `markdown`, `json`, `csv`) make results easier to read.

- `.import --csv data.csv product` loads a **CSV** file: a table saved as plain text, one row per line, values separated by commas. If the table doesn't exist yet, the file's first line becomes the column names.
- `.once out.csv` sends the next query's result to a file; `.output out.txt` sends all results there until you switch back with `.output`.

- `.read file.sql` runs a file of SQL statements; `.dump` writes out the whole database as SQL, a simple **backup**.
- `.open other.db` switches files; `.quit` exits; `.help` lists everything.

From the terminal you can also run a single statement, `sqlite3 shop.db "SELECT count(*) FROM product;"`, or feed in a whole file of SQL: `sqlite3 shop.db < schema.sql`.

Apps with windows and buttons, such as DB Browser for SQLite, open the same files. Some computers come with an old version of `sqlite3`; download a current one from sqlite.org if a newer feature is missing.
concepts.code:
$ sqlite3 shop.db
sqlite> CREATE TABLE product (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT, price REAL);
sqlite> INSERT INTO product (name, price) VALUES ('pen', 1.5), ('book', 12);
sqlite> .headers on
sqlite> .mode box
sqlite> SELECT * FROM product;
┌────┬──────┬───────┐
│ id │ name │ price │
├────┼──────┼───────┤
│ 1  │ pen  │ 1.5   │
│ 2  │ book │ 12.0  │
└────┴──────┴───────┘
sqlite> .tables
product
sqlite> .import --csv more_products.csv product
sqlite> .quit

$ sqlite3 shop.db .dump > backup.sql      # save the whole database as SQL in backup.sql
takeaways: sqlite3 file.db opens or creates a database
Dot-commands (.tables, .schema, .mode, .import) belong to the sqlite3 tool, not to SQL
.dump saves the whole database as SQL
pitfalls: Running .import into an existing table from a CSV whose first line holds column names: that line becomes a data row (add --skip 1).

options: Prints the CREATE statement for product
quiz.explain: .schema shows the SQL that defines the named table and its indexes.

concepts.name: Python's sqlite3 module
concepts.summary: Use SQLite from Python programs with the built-in sqlite3 module: connect, run SQL with placeholders, read rows and commit.
concepts.why: sqlite3 comes with Python, so it's the quickest way to give any Python program a real database.
concepts.body:
Python is a popular programming language, and SQLite comes built in: Python includes a **module** (a bundle of ready-made code) called `sqlite3`, so there's nothing to install. This lesson covers the handful of calls you need; the comments in the example say what each line does.

`con = sqlite3.connect("app.db")` opens the file and keeps the connection under the name `con`. Use `":memory:"` instead of a file name for a throwaway database.

`con.execute(sql, values)` runs one statement. For a query, `fetchone()` on the result gives the next row and `fetchall()` gives all of them. Each row comes back as a **tuple**: a fixed list of values in brackets, like `(1, 'Ani')`. Set `con.row_factory = sqlite3.Row` to read values by column name instead, as in `row["name"]`.

**Never paste values into the SQL text.** Write a `?` placeholder where each value goes and pass the values separately: `con.execute("SELECT * FROM user WHERE city = ?", (city,))`. SQLite then treats them strictly as data. Building the text yourself breaks on names like O'Brien and lets an attacker slip in SQL of their own (**SQL injection**). Named placeholders such as `:city` work too, with the values given by name.

`con.executemany(sql, rows)` runs one statement for many rows, efficiently.

Saving changes: by default the module starts a transaction for you before `INSERT`, `UPDATE`, `DELETE` and `REPLACE`, and nothing is saved until you call `con.commit()`. Closing without committing throws the changes away. A `with con:` block commits if everything inside it succeeds and rolls back if an error happens, but it does **not** close the connection. (Python 3.12 added an `autocommit` option that changes this; see the Transactions lesson.)

`cur.lastrowid` gives the id of the row just inserted and `cur.rowcount` how many rows a statement changed. Call `con.close()` when you're done.
concepts.code:
import sqlite3                                   # load the module

con = sqlite3.connect(":memory:")                 # open a throwaway database
con.row_factory = sqlite3.Row                    # rows readable by column name
con.execute("CREATE TABLE user (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT, city TEXT)")

with con:                                        # commit if the block succeeds
    cur = con.execute("INSERT INTO user (name, city) VALUES (?, ?)", ("Ani", "Yerevan"))
    print(cur.lastrowid)                         # 1
    con.executemany("INSERT INTO user (name, city) VALUES (?, ?)",
                    [("Davit", "Gyumri"), ("O'Brien", "Dublin")])   # the quote is safe

for row in con.execute("SELECT id, name FROM user WHERE city = :c", {"c": "Gyumri"}):
    print(row["id"], row["name"])                # 2 Davit

name = "x' OR '1'='1"                            # an attack attempt is just data
print(con.execute("SELECT count(*) FROM user WHERE name = ?", (name,)).fetchone()[0])  # 0
con.close()
takeaways: Use ? or :name placeholders, never paste values into the SQL text
Changes need con.commit() (or a with con: block)
with con: commits or rolls back but doesn't close the connection
pitfalls: Forgetting to commit, so inserts silently disappear when the program exits.

quiz.q: A script inserts rows with con.execute() and exits without commit() or a with block. What is saved?
options: The rows are saved to a journal and replayed later
Nothing: the implicit transaction is rolled back
quiz.explain: By default the module opened a transaction for you, and closing without commit() throws it away.

concepts.name: Dynamic typing and type affinity
concepts.summary: SQLite stores a type with each value; declared column types only express an affinity, not a rule.
concepts.why: SQLite's relaxed typing surprises everyone coming from other databases and lets wrong data slip in unnoticed.
concepts.body:
Most databases enforce a column's data type. SQLite, in ordinary tables, does not: each *value* carries its own type, and a column can hold values of any type. This is called **dynamic typing**. Every value has one of five **storage classes**: `NULL`, `INTEGER`, `REAL` (a decimal number), `TEXT` or `BLOB` (raw bytes, kept exactly as given).

The type you declare gives the column a **type affinity**: a preferred type that SQLite converts values towards when it can. The rules look at the type's name:

- Contains `INT` → **INTEGER** affinity.
- Contains `CHAR`, `CLOB` or `TEXT` → **TEXT**.
- Contains `BLOB`, or no type at all → **BLOB** (stored as given).
- Contains `REAL`, `FLOA` or `DOUB` → **REAL**.
- Anything else (e.g. `NUMERIC`, `DECIMAL`, `BOOLEAN`, `DATE`) → **NUMERIC**.

So in an `INTEGER` column, the text `'42'` is converted to the number 42, but `'hello'` is stored as text, without complaint. `VARCHAR(10)` has TEXT affinity and the 10 is ignored: longer text is stored in full.

There are no separate date or yes/no types. Store dates as text in the standard ISO 8601 form (`'2026-05-03 14:00:00'`) or as a Unix timestamp (seconds since 1970), and use the date functions (`date()`, `datetime()`, `strftime()`, `unixepoch()`). Yes/no values are the numbers 0 and 1; `TRUE` and `FALSE` are just other names for them.

`typeof(x)` shows a value's actual storage class. If you want types enforced, use `CHECK` constraints or **STRICT** tables (a later lesson).
takeaways: Values have storage classes; columns only have an affinity
VARCHAR(n) lengths are not enforced
Dates are text, integers or reals; booleans are 0/1
pitfalls: Relying on a column type to reject bad data in a non-STRICT table.

quiz.q: In a non-STRICT table, what happens when you insert 'abc' into a column declared INTEGER?
options: It is stored as the text 'abc'
quiz.explain: The column's affinity converts text only when it looks like a number; otherwise the value is kept as TEXT.

concepts.name: rowid, INTEGER PRIMARY KEY and AUTOINCREMENT
concepts.summary: Every ordinary SQLite table has a hidden whole-number key, the rowid; a column declared INTEGER PRIMARY KEY becomes another name for it.
concepts.why: Choosing the key form changes storage, id reuse and performance in ways specific to SQLite.
concepts.body:
Every ordinary SQLite table has a hidden whole-number key, the **rowid**. The table's rows are stored sorted by rowid, like entries in a phone book, so finding a row by its rowid is the fastest lookup there is. You can select it as `rowid`.

If you declare a column exactly as `INTEGER PRIMARY KEY`, that column becomes **another name for the rowid** rather than a separate column. Insert `NULL` (or leave it out) and SQLite picks a value: normally one more than the current largest. The exact spelling matters: `INT PRIMARY KEY` or `BIGINT PRIMARY KEY` is *not* the rowid; it creates an ordinary column with a separate unique index.

Plain `INTEGER PRIMARY KEY` can **reuse** ids: if you delete the row with the largest id, the next insert may get the same id again. Adding **AUTOINCREMENT** guarantees ids are never reused, by keeping a record in a built-in table called `sqlite_sequence`. That costs a little extra work per insert, so SQLite's documentation recommends it only when never reusing an id really matters.

`WITHOUT ROWID` tables are stored sorted by the declared primary key instead. They save space for tables whose key isn't a single whole number and whose rows are small, such as a table that only links posts to tags with the key `(post_id, tag)`. They require an explicit `PRIMARY KEY`.

To get the new rowid after an insert: `last_insert_rowid()` in SQL, or add `RETURNING id` to the end of the `INSERT` and it hands the new id back.
takeaways: INTEGER PRIMARY KEY (exact spelling) is another name for the rowid
Without AUTOINCREMENT, the largest deleted id can be reused
WITHOUT ROWID suits small rows whose key isn't a single whole number
pitfalls: Declaring INT PRIMARY KEY and expecting automatic ids: only INTEGER PRIMARY KEY aliases the rowid.

quiz.q: Which declaration makes id an alias for the rowid?
quiz.explain: Only the exact type name INTEGER with PRIMARY KEY makes the column another name for the rowid.

concepts.name: STRICT tables and CHECK constraints
concepts.summary: Make SQLite enforce column types with STRICT tables (3.37+) and add CHECK constraints for the rest.
concepts.why: STRICT tables make SQLite check column types the way other databases do, while keeping its simplicity.
concepts.body:
Since SQLite 3.37, adding the keyword **STRICT** after a `CREATE TABLE` statement turns on rigid typing for that table:

- Each column must be declared with one of `INT`, `INTEGER`, `REAL`, `TEXT`, `BLOB` or `ANY`.
- Inserting a value that can't be losslessly converted to the column's type raises an error: `cannot store TEXT value in INTEGER column`. Text like `'42'` is still converted to the integer 42, since that is lossless.
- `ANY` columns accept anything and keep it exactly as given.
- `INTEGER PRIMARY KEY` columns still alias the rowid, and `PRIMARY KEY` columns are implicitly `NOT NULL`.

STRICT doesn't add date or boolean types, nor length limits on text. For those, use **CHECK constraints**, which SQLite has always enforced:

- `CHECK (length(code) = 3)`
- `CHECK (active IN (0, 1))`
- `CHECK (created_at IS datetime(created_at))` to accept only valid ISO 8601 date-times.

Combine `STRICT` with `WITHOUT ROWID` as `) STRICT, WITHOUT ROWID;`. Older SQLite versions can't open databases containing STRICT tables, so check the minimum version your users have (from Python, `sqlite3.sqlite_version` tells you which SQLite you have).

For new schemas, STRICT tables are a cheap way to catch mistakes early.
concepts.code:
import sqlite3

con = sqlite3.connect(":memory:")
con.execute('''
    CREATE TABLE account (
        id      INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
        code    TEXT NOT NULL CHECK (length(code) = 3),
        balance INTEGER NOT NULL,
        active  INTEGER NOT NULL DEFAULT 1 CHECK (active IN (0, 1)),
        meta    ANY
    ) STRICT
''')
con.execute("INSERT INTO account (code, balance, meta) VALUES ('AMD', '100', 1.5)")
print(con.execute("SELECT balance, typeof(balance) FROM account").fetchone())  # (100, 'integer')

for bad in [("USD", "lots"), ("EURO", 5)]:
    try:
        con.execute("INSERT INTO account (code, balance) VALUES (?, ?)", bad)
    except sqlite3.Error as e:
        print(type(e).__name__, e)
# IntegrityError cannot store TEXT value in INTEGER column account.balance
# IntegrityError CHECK constraint failed: length(code) = 3
takeaways: STRICT enforces INT, INTEGER, REAL, TEXT, BLOB or ANY per column
Lossless conversions like '42' -> 42 still happen
Use CHECK constraints for lengths, booleans and date formats
pitfalls: Shipping a database with STRICT tables to clients running SQLite older than 3.37.

quiz.q: In a STRICT table, inserting the text '42' into an INTEGER column...
quiz.explain: The text converts losslessly to an integer, so STRICT accepts and converts it.

concepts.name: Foreign keys and essential PRAGMAs
concepts.summary: Turn on foreign key enforcement per connection and know the PRAGMAs every SQLite app should set.
concepts.why: Foreign keys are off by default in SQLite, so many apps believe they're protected when they aren't.
concepts.body:
SQLite accepts `REFERENCES` clauses but, so that old apps keep working, **doesn't enforce foreign keys unless you enable them** on each connection: `PRAGMA foreign_keys = ON`. The setting isn't stored in the database file; every new connection starts with it off. It also can't be changed inside a transaction.

**PRAGMA** statements read or change SQLite settings and inspect the database. The ones worth knowing:

- `PRAGMA foreign_keys = ON;` — enforce references (per connection).
- `PRAGMA journal_mode = WAL;` — lets readers and the writer work at the same time; stored in the file (a later lesson).
- `PRAGMA busy_timeout = 5000;` — wait up to 5 s for locks instead of failing at once.
- `PRAGMA synchronous = NORMAL;` — a common speed/durability trade-off with WAL.
- `PRAGMA foreign_key_check;` — list existing rows that violate foreign keys (useful after enabling them on an old database).
- `PRAGMA integrity_check;` — verify the file's structure.
- `PRAGMA table_info(t);` / `PRAGMA index_list(t);` — describe a table's columns and indexes, also available as table-valued functions: `SELECT * FROM pragma_table_info('t')`.
- `PRAGMA user_version;` — an integer you can use for schema versioning.

Put the per-connection PRAGMAs in one function that opens connections, so no code path forgets them.
takeaways: Foreign keys are off by default: PRAGMA foreign_keys = ON on every connection
PRAGMAs configure the connection or inspect the database
Centralise connection setup so every connection gets the same PRAGMAs
pitfalls: Enabling foreign keys once in the sqlite3 tool and assuming the application's connections enforce them too.

quiz.q: You enabled PRAGMA foreign_keys = ON in the sqlite3 shell yesterday. Does your app's new connection enforce foreign keys?
options: No, it must be enabled on each connection
Yes, the setting is saved in the file
quiz.explain: foreign_keys is a per-connection setting that defaults to off.

concepts.name: Transactions, locking and SQLITE_BUSY
concepts.summary: Use DEFERRED, IMMEDIATE and EXCLUSIVE transactions, avoid 'database is locked', and control Python's transaction handling.
concepts.why: Understanding SQLite's one-writer lock is the key to using it reliably when several programs, or several parts of one program, share a database.
concepts.body:
SQLite allows many readers but only **one writer at a time** for the whole database. Transactions start with:

- `BEGIN` (= `BEGIN DEFERRED`): takes no lock until the first read or write. A transaction that reads and then writes must *upgrade* its lock. If another connection is writing, that upgrade can fail at once with **SQLITE_BUSY** ('database is locked'). Waiting wouldn't help, because the two could end up waiting for each other forever (a deadlock).
- `BEGIN IMMEDIATE`: takes the write lock right away, waiting for it if needed. Use it for any transaction that will write; it avoids the failed upgrade.
- `BEGIN EXCLUSIVE`: in the default journal mode also blocks readers; in WAL mode (next lesson) it behaves like IMMEDIATE.

Set a **busy timeout** so connections wait for a lock for a while instead of failing at once: Python's `sqlite3.connect(path, timeout=5.0)` (5 seconds is the default) or `PRAGMA busy_timeout`.

Python's transaction control:

- Old default: the module quietly issues `BEGIN` (deferred) before data-changing statements; `isolation_level="IMMEDIATE"` makes that `BEGIN IMMEDIATE`, and `isolation_level=None` means you write `BEGIN` and `COMMIT` yourself.
- Python 3.12+: `autocommit=False` gives the behaviour Python's database standard (PEP 249) describes: a transaction is always open, and `commit()` starts the next one. `autocommit=True` leaves everything to the SQL you write.

Keep write transactions short: while one is open, every other writer waits.
concepts.code:
import sqlite3, os, tempfile

path = os.path.join(tempfile.mkdtemp(), "app.db")
setup = sqlite3.connect(path)
setup.execute("CREATE TABLE counter (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, n INTEGER)")
setup.execute("INSERT INTO counter VALUES (1, 0)")
setup.commit()

a = sqlite3.connect(path, isolation_level=None)          # manual transactions
b = sqlite3.connect(path, isolation_level=None, timeout=0.1)

a.execute("BEGIN IMMEDIATE")                              # a holds the write lock
a.execute("UPDATE counter SET n = n + 1 WHERE id = 1")
try:
    b.execute("BEGIN IMMEDIATE")                          # waits 0.1 s, then fails
except sqlite3.OperationalError as e:
    print(e)                                              # database is locked
print(b.execute("SELECT n FROM counter").fetchone())      # (0,) readers still work
a.execute("COMMIT")
b.execute("BEGIN IMMEDIATE"); b.execute("UPDATE counter SET n = n + 1"); b.execute("COMMIT")
print(b.execute("SELECT n FROM counter").fetchone())      # (2,)
takeaways: One writer at a time; readers continue
Use BEGIN IMMEDIATE for transactions that will write
Set a busy timeout so writers wait instead of failing
pitfalls: Starting a read-then-write transaction with plain BEGIN and getting random 'database is locked' errors under load.

quiz.q: Why prefer BEGIN IMMEDIATE for a transaction that reads and then writes?
options: It takes the write lock up front, avoiding a failed lock upgrade later
It lets two writers run at once
quiz.explain: A deferred transaction that must upgrade to a write lock while another writer is active fails with SQLITE_BUSY.

concepts.name: ALTER TABLE limits and migrations
concepts.summary: Work within SQLite's limited ALTER TABLE, rebuild tables safely, and version schemas with user_version.
concepts.why: Schema changes in SQLite need a specific procedure; doing it naively loses data or breaks foreign keys.
concepts.body:
SQLite's `ALTER TABLE` supports only a few operations:

- `RENAME TO new_name` (rename the table),
- `RENAME COLUMN old TO new`,
- `ADD COLUMN` (with restrictions: no `PRIMARY KEY` or `UNIQUE`, and a `NOT NULL` column needs a non-NULL default),
- `DROP COLUMN` (3.35+; fails if the column is indexed, part of a key, or used by a constraint, view or trigger, which is code the database runs automatically when rows change).

Anything else (changing a type, adding a constraint, changing a default) needs a **table rebuild**: build a new table and copy the rows over. The documented safe procedure, in short:

1. `PRAGMA foreign_keys = OFF` (outside the transaction), then `BEGIN`.
2. `CREATE TABLE new_t (...)` with the desired definition.
3. `INSERT INTO new_t SELECT ... FROM t`.
4. `DROP TABLE t; ALTER TABLE new_t RENAME TO t;`
5. Recreate indexes, triggers and views on `t`.
6. `PRAGMA foreign_key_check;` then `COMMIT` and turn foreign keys back on.

Because SQLite DDL is transactional, a failure mid-way rolls back cleanly.

To track which migrations have run, store an integer in the file header with `PRAGMA user_version = n` and read it at startup: apply each migration whose number is higher, in a transaction, then bump the version. In Python projects that use SQLAlchemy, the Alembic tool does this for you, with a 'batch' mode that performs rebuilds.
takeaways: ALTER TABLE can rename, add and drop columns, little else
Other changes need the create-copy-drop-rename rebuild
PRAGMA user_version is a simple, built-in migration counter
pitfalls: Rebuilding a table with foreign keys still ON, which can cascade deletes into child tables when the old table is dropped.

quiz.q: You need to add a CHECK constraint to an existing SQLite table. How?
options: Rebuild the table: create new, copy, drop old, rename
quiz.explain: SQLite's ALTER TABLE doesn't support adding constraints, so the table must be rebuilt.

concepts.name: JSON, upserts and RETURNING
concepts.summary: Query JSON with -> and ->>, turn JSON lists into rows with json_each, and write with ON CONFLICT upserts and RETURNING.
concepts.why: These newer features let SQLite handle flexible data, and writes that are safe to repeat, in single statements.
concepts.body:
**JSON** is a text format for structured data: `{"brand": "Acme", "tags": ["sale", "new"]}` holds named values in curly braces and lists in square brackets. SQLite stores JSON as ordinary text (or, since 3.45, in a compact binary form called **jsonb**, through the `jsonb_*` functions) and has a rich set of JSON functions.

- `doc -> '$.address'` returns JSON text; `doc ->> '$.address.city'` returns a plain SQL value (text, number or NULL). Both arrived in 3.38; `json_extract()` works in every version.
- `json_each(doc, '$.tags')` produces one row per item of a JSON list, so you can join and filter on it.
- `json_set`, `json_insert`, `json_replace`, `json_remove` return changed documents; `json_object` and `json_group_array` build JSON from rows.
- Index a value inside JSON with an **expression index** (an index on a calculated value): `CREATE INDEX ix ON t (doc ->> '$.sku')`. Queries that use the same expression can use it.

**Upsert** (3.24+), insert-or-update, is written the same way as in PostgreSQL: `INSERT ... ON CONFLICT (col) DO UPDATE SET qty = qty + excluded.qty`, or `DO NOTHING`. The conflict columns must have a unique index or be the primary key. Older SQLite code uses `INSERT OR REPLACE`, which deletes and re-inserts the row (so delete triggers fire, linked rows may be deleted, and the row gets a new rowid). Prefer `ON CONFLICT`.

**RETURNING** (3.35+) makes `INSERT`, `UPDATE` and `DELETE` hand back the rows they changed, including generated ids and default values, saving a second query.
concepts.code:
import sqlite3, json

con = sqlite3.connect(":memory:")
con.execute("CREATE TABLE product (sku TEXT PRIMARY KEY, qty INTEGER, doc TEXT)")
con.execute("CREATE INDEX product_brand ON product (doc ->> '$.brand')")
con.execute("INSERT INTO product VALUES (?, ?, ?)",
            ("A1", 5, json.dumps({"brand": "Acme", "tags": ["sale", "new"]})))

print(con.execute("SELECT doc -> '$.tags', doc ->> '$.brand' FROM product").fetchone())
# ('["sale","new"]', 'Acme')
print(con.execute('''SELECT p.sku, t.value FROM product p, json_each(p.doc, '$.tags') t
                     WHERE t.value = 'sale' ''').fetchall())     # [('A1', 'sale')]

row = con.execute('''INSERT INTO product (sku, qty) VALUES ('A1', 3)
                     ON CONFLICT (sku) DO UPDATE SET qty = qty + excluded.qty
                     RETURNING sku, qty''').fetchone()
print(row)                                                      # ('A1', 8)
takeaways: -> returns JSON, ->> returns a plain SQL value
json_each turns JSON lists into rows
Prefer ON CONFLICT ... DO UPDATE over INSERT OR REPLACE; RETURNING saves a query
pitfalls: Using INSERT OR REPLACE as an upsert and losing columns not included in the insert.

quiz.q: What does INSERT OR REPLACE do when the key already exists?
options: Deletes the existing row and inserts a new one
quiz.explain: REPLACE resolves the conflict by deleting the old row, so unspecified columns get defaults and delete triggers can fire.

concepts.name: Journal modes and WAL
concepts.summary: Switch to write-ahead logging so readers and the writer don't block each other, and understand checkpoints.
concepts.why: WAL mode is the single biggest improvement for SQLite concurrency and write speed in most apps.
concepts.body:
SQLite needs a journal (a side file) to make transactions all-or-nothing. The default **rollback journal** (`journal_mode = DELETE`) copies the original pages to a `-journal` file before changing the database. While a writer commits, it needs an exclusive lock, so readers and the writer block each other.

**WAL mode** (`PRAGMA journal_mode = WAL`) inverts this: changes are *appended* to a separate `-wal` file, and the main database file is updated later. Benefits:

- **Readers don't block the writer and the writer doesn't block readers.** Each reader sees a consistent snapshot as of when its read transaction began.
- Writes are usually faster: changes are added at the end of one file, with fewer forced writes to disk, especially with `PRAGMA synchronous = NORMAL`, which in WAL mode can lose the most recent commits on power loss but never corrupts the database.

There is still only **one writer at a time**.

Periodically the WAL content is copied back into the database file by a **checkpoint** — automatically when the WAL reaches about 1000 pages (`wal_autocheckpoint`), or manually with `PRAGMA wal_checkpoint(TRUNCATE)`. A reader that never finishes can prevent the checkpoint from completing, letting the WAL grow without bound.

Details to know: WAL mode is remembered in the file, so set it once. It creates `-wal` and `-shm` files next to the database; copy them along with it, or use the backup API (Expert lesson). All programs using the database must be on the **same machine**: WAL coordinates them through shared memory, which doesn't work across network drives.
concepts.code:
import sqlite3, os, tempfile

path = os.path.join(tempfile.mkdtemp(), "app.db")
w = sqlite3.connect(path, isolation_level=None)
print(w.execute("PRAGMA journal_mode = WAL").fetchone())     # ('wal',)
w.execute("PRAGMA synchronous = NORMAL")
w.execute("CREATE TABLE log (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, msg TEXT)")
w.execute("INSERT INTO log (msg) VALUES ('first')")

r = sqlite3.connect(path, isolation_level=None)
r.execute("BEGIN")                                            # reader snapshot
print(r.execute("SELECT count(*) FROM log").fetchone())       # (1,)

w.execute("BEGIN IMMEDIATE")                                  # writer not blocked
w.execute("INSERT INTO log (msg) VALUES ('second')")
w.execute("COMMIT")
print(r.execute("SELECT count(*) FROM log").fetchone())       # (1,) same snapshot
r.execute("COMMIT")
print(r.execute("SELECT count(*) FROM log").fetchone())       # (2,)

print(w.execute("PRAGMA wal_checkpoint(TRUNCATE)").fetchone())   # (0, 0, 0)
print(sorted(os.listdir(os.path.dirname(path))))   # ['app.db', 'app.db-shm', 'app.db-wal']
takeaways: WAL: readers and the single writer don't block each other
synchronous=NORMAL with WAL is fast and corruption-safe
Checkpoints move WAL content into the database; long readers can stall them
pitfalls: Copying only app.db while the app runs in WAL mode, leaving recent commits behind in app.db-wal.

quiz.q: In WAL mode, what happens to a reader while a write transaction commits?
options: It is blocked until the commit finishes
It continues reading its consistent snapshot
quiz.explain: WAL readers use the database plus the WAL up to their snapshot point, independent of the writer.

concepts.name: Indexes and EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN
concepts.summary: Read EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN output, design indexes for SQLite's planner, and keep statistics fresh with ANALYZE and PRAGMA optimize.
concepts.why: A missing index makes SQLite scan whole tables; one well-chosen index can make a query thousands of times faster.
concepts.body:
`EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN` shows how SQLite will run a statement, one line per step:

- `SCAN t` — reads the whole table.
- `SEARCH t USING INDEX ix (col=?)` — uses an index to find rows.
- `SEARCH t USING INTEGER PRIMARY KEY (rowid=?)` — direct rowid lookup, the fastest.
- `USING COVERING INDEX` — the index has all needed columns, so the table isn't touched.
- `USE TEMP B-TREE FOR ORDER BY` — an extra sort step an index could avoid.

Indexes in SQLite follow the usual B-tree rules: a composite index serves queries on its leftmost columns, equality columns go first and the range or sort column last. Partial indexes (only rows matching a `WHERE` clause) and expression indexes (on a calculated value) are supported. Every index entry also stores the rowid.

SQLite's planner is cost-based but has little information by default. **`ANALYZE`** gathers statistics into `sqlite_stat1` (and `sqlite_stat4` if your SQLite build includes it) to help it choose between indexes. The recommended routine is **`PRAGMA optimize`**, which runs `ANALYZE` only where it's likely to help: run it periodically, or just before closing long-lived connections.

Other performance basics: wrap bulk inserts in one transaction (otherwise each statement is its own transaction, with its own forced write to disk), reuse connections, and use `executemany`. With those, SQLite handles hundreds of thousands of inserts per second.
concepts.code:
import sqlite3

con = sqlite3.connect(":memory:")
con.execute("CREATE TABLE orders (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, customer INTEGER, total REAL, day TEXT)")
with con:      # one transaction for the bulk insert
    con.executemany("INSERT INTO orders (customer, total, day) VALUES (?, ?, ?)",
                    ((i % 1000, i * 0.5, f"2026-05-{i % 28 + 1:02d}") for i in range(100_000)))

q = "SELECT day, total FROM orders WHERE customer = 42 ORDER BY day"
plan = lambda: [row[3] for row in con.execute("EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN " + q)]
print(plan())   # ['SCAN orders', 'USE TEMP B-TREE FOR ORDER BY']

con.execute("CREATE INDEX orders_customer_day ON orders (customer, day, total)")
print(plan())   # ['SEARCH orders USING COVERING INDEX orders_customer_day (customer=?)']

con.execute("PRAGMA optimize")
print(con.execute("EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN SELECT * FROM orders WHERE id = 7").fetchall()[0][3])
# SEARCH orders USING INTEGER PRIMARY KEY (rowid=?)
takeaways: SCAN = full table read; SEARCH = index or rowid lookup
Composite and covering indexes remove scans and temp B-tree sorts
Batch writes in one transaction; run PRAGMA optimize periodically
pitfalls: Inserting thousands of rows without a transaction around them, paying a forced disk write per row.

quiz.q: EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN shows 'USE TEMP B-TREE FOR ORDER BY'. What does it mean?
options: SQLite must sort results itself because no index provides the order
The query uses a covering index
A temporary table is being written to disk permanently
quiz.explain: The rows don't come out of an index in the requested order, so SQLite builds a temporary B-tree to sort them.

concepts.name: Full-text search with FTS5
concepts.summary: Build fast word search with FTS5 virtual tables, MATCH queries, bm25 ranking and highlight snippets.
concepts.why: FTS5 gives apps proper search over notes, messages or documents with no extra service.
concepts.body:
`LIKE '%word%'` scans every row and can't rank results. **FTS5** is SQLite's full-text search extension (included in most builds, including Python's). It keeps an index like the one at the back of a book: for each word (token), the rows that contain it.

- Create a **virtual table**: `CREATE VIRTUAL TABLE doc_fts USING fts5(title, body)`. All columns are text and untyped.
- Query with `MATCH`: `WHERE doc_fts MATCH 'sqlite AND wal'`. The query syntax supports implicit AND between terms, `OR`, `NOT`, `"exact phrases"`, prefix search `data*`, column filters `title:sqlite` and `NEAR(a b, 5)`.
- Rank with the hidden `rank` column (`ORDER BY rank`), which defaults to **bm25**; `bm25(doc_fts, 10.0, 1.0)` weights the title higher.
- `highlight(doc_fts, 1, '[', ']')` and `snippet(...)` produce marked-up excerpts.
- Tokenizers, the rules for splitting text into words: `unicode61` (default; ignores case and accents), `porter`, which cuts English words down to a common root so "run", "runs" and "running" all match each other (`tokenize='porter unicode61'`), and `trigram`, which indexes every run of three characters so a search can match any part of a word, like `LIKE '%ite%'` but using the index.

To avoid storing text twice, use an **external-content** table (`content='docs', content_rowid='id'`) that indexes rows of a normal table; then you keep the index in sync with triggers (code the database runs automatically) on that table.

User input can contain characters that are FTS5 syntax, so a raw search string may raise a syntax error; quote it as a phrase (double the `"` characters inside) when you don't want operators.
concepts.code:
import sqlite3

con = sqlite3.connect(":memory:")
con.execute("CREATE VIRTUAL TABLE note USING fts5(title, body, tokenize='porter unicode61')")
con.executemany("INSERT INTO note (title, body) VALUES (?, ?)", [
    ("Tuning SQLite", "Enable WAL mode and run PRAGMA optimize."),
    ("Indexes", "Covering indexes avoid table lookups when running queries."),
    ("Shopping", "Milk, bread and eggs."),
])
q = "SELECT title FROM note WHERE note MATCH ? ORDER BY rank"
print(con.execute(q, ("run",)).fetchall())          # porter: 'run' matches 'running' and 'run'
# [('Tuning SQLite',), ('Indexes',)]   (order by bm25 score)
print(con.execute(q, ("title:sqlite OR eggs",)).fetchall())
# [('Shopping',), ('Tuning SQLite',)]

print(con.execute('''SELECT highlight(note, 1, '[', ']') FROM note
                     WHERE note MATCH 'wal' ''').fetchone()[0])
# Enable [WAL] mode and run PRAGMA optimize.

user_input = 'C++ "fast"'
safe = '"' + user_input.replace('"', '""') + '"'      # treat as a phrase
print(con.execute(q, (safe,)).fetchall())            # [] and no syntax error
takeaways: FTS5 virtual tables + MATCH give indexed word search
ORDER BY rank sorts by bm25 relevance
Quote user input as a phrase to avoid FTS5 syntax errors
pitfalls: Passing raw user input to MATCH and crashing on characters like quotes or hyphens.

quiz.q: Why can't LIKE '%term%' replace FTS5 for search?
options: It scans every row and can't rank results by relevance
LIKE doesn't work on TEXT columns
quiz.explain: LIKE with a leading wildcard can't use an index and has no notion of relevance.

concepts.name: The file format: pages, B-trees and VACUUM
concepts.summary: How a SQLite file is organised into pages and B-trees, what the freelist is, and when VACUUM helps.
concepts.why: Knowing the on-disk layout explains file size, fragmentation and many performance characteristics.
concepts.body:
A SQLite database file is an array of fixed-size **pages** (4096 bytes by default, any power of two from 512 to 65536, set with `PRAGMA page_size` before the database is populated or followed by `VACUUM`). Page 1 starts with a 100-byte header — the magic string `SQLite format 3`, page size, file change counter, `user_version`, a schema version counter and more.

Every table is a **table B-tree** keyed by rowid: interior pages hold keys and child pointers; leaf pages hold the full rows. Every index (and every `WITHOUT ROWID` table) is an **index B-tree** whose keys are the indexed values plus the rowid. The `sqlite_schema` table on page 1 records each object's SQL and **root page**. Rows too large for a page spill into chains of **overflow pages**.

Records are stored in a compact format: a header of type codes followed by values. Small integers take one byte or even zero (the constants 0 and 1 live in the header), which is why SQLite files are compact.

When you delete data, freed pages go onto the **freelist** and are reused, but the file doesn't shrink. **`VACUUM`** rebuilds the database into a fresh file, removing free pages and defragmenting B-trees. It needs free disk space up to twice the database size and an exclusive lock. `PRAGMA auto_vacuum = INCREMENTAL` plus `PRAGMA incremental_vacuum` returns free pages without a full rebuild (it must be set before tables are created, or followed by a VACUUM). `VACUUM INTO 'copy.db'` writes a compacted copy and is also a handy backup.
concepts.code:
import sqlite3, os, tempfile

path = os.path.join(tempfile.mkdtemp(), "big.db")
con = sqlite3.connect(path)
con.execute("CREATE TABLE blob (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, data TEXT)")
with con:
    con.executemany("INSERT INTO blob (data) VALUES (?)", (("x" * 500,) for _ in range(20000)))
pragma = lambda p: con.execute(f"PRAGMA {p}").fetchone()[0]
print(pragma("page_size"), pragma("page_count"), pragma("freelist_count"))  # 4096 2508 0

with con:
    con.execute("DELETE FROM blob WHERE id <= 10000")
print(pragma("page_count"), pragma("freelist_count"))   # 2508 1253: same size, pages on the freelist
print(os.path.getsize(path) // 1024, "KiB")             # file did not shrink

con.execute("VACUUM")
print(pragma("page_count"), pragma("freelist_count"))   # 1255 0
print(open(path, "rb").read(16))                        # b'SQLite format 3\x00'
takeaways: The file is an array of pages; tables and indexes are B-trees
Deleted space goes to the freelist; the file doesn't shrink
VACUUM rebuilds and compacts; VACUUM INTO makes a compact copy
pitfalls: Running VACUUM on a large database without enough free disk space for a full copy.

quiz.q: After deleting half the rows, the database file is the same size. Why?
options: The WAL file holds the deleted rows
Freed pages go to the freelist for reuse instead of being returned to the OS
quiz.explain: SQLite reuses free pages; only VACUUM (or auto_vacuum) shrinks the file.

concepts.name: The bytecode engine (VDBE)
concepts.summary: SQLite compiles each SQL statement into a bytecode program; EXPLAIN shows it and prepared statements reuse it.
concepts.why: Understanding statement compilation explains the value of parameters, statement caching and how SQLite executes queries.
concepts.body:
Inside, SQLite works like a small compiler plus an interpreter. When you prepare a statement (`sqlite3_prepare_v2` in C; the Python module does this for you), SQLite splits the SQL into words, works out its structure, plans it, and generates a program of simple instructions (**bytecode**). Its built-in interpreter, the **VDBE** (virtual database engine), runs that program. Running the statement means stepping through that program: each `sqlite3_step()` executes opcodes until a result row is ready or the program halts.

`EXPLAIN SELECT ...` (without `QUERY PLAN`) lists the bytecode. Typical opcodes:

- `Init`, `Transaction`, `Goto` — set-up and starting a read or write transaction.
- `OpenRead` / `OpenWrite` — open a cursor on a B-tree by its root page.
- `Rewind` / `Next` — loop over a table; `SeekGE`, `IdxGT`, `SeekRowid` — positioned index lookups.
- `Column`, `Rowid` — read values from the current row; `ResultRow` — emit a row.
- `Halt` — end of program.

Compilation is relatively expensive compared with executing a simple statement, so reusing **prepared statements** matters. Python's `sqlite3` keeps a per-connection statement cache (`cached_statements`, 128 by default), keyed by the SQL text. That is another reason to use parameters: `WHERE id = ?` is compiled once and reused, whereas formatting values into the SQL creates a new statement every time.

Opcodes and their output can change between SQLite versions; use `EXPLAIN` output to investigate, not as something your code depends on.
concepts.code:
import sqlite3

con = sqlite3.connect(":memory:")
con.execute("CREATE TABLE t (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT)")
con.execute("CREATE INDEX t_name ON t (name)")

for addr, opcode, p1, p2, p3, p4, p5, comment in con.execute(
        "EXPLAIN SELECT id FROM t WHERE name = ?", ("x",)):
    print(addr, opcode, p1, p2, p3)
# 0 Init 0 ...
# ... OpenRead ...             cursor on the t_name index B-tree
# ... SeekGE ...               jump to the first entry >= ?
# ... IdxGT ...                stop when past the value
# ... IdxRowid ...             read the rowid stored in the index entry
# ... ResultRow ...            emit one row
# ... Halt ...
# (exact addresses and operands vary by SQLite version)

for i in range(1000):          # compiled once, then served from the statement cache
    con.execute("SELECT name FROM t WHERE id = ?", (i,))
takeaways: SQL is compiled to VDBE bytecode, then executed step by step
EXPLAIN shows the bytecode; EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN the high-level plan
Parameters let compiled statements be cached and reused
pitfalls: Formatting values into SQL strings, which defeats the statement cache as well as being unsafe.

quiz.q: Why does using ? parameters improve performance in a loop?
options: The same SQL text can reuse its compiled bytecode from the statement cache
quiz.explain: Identical SQL text hits the cached prepared statement, avoiding recompilation.

concepts.name: Running SQLite in production
concepts.summary: Configure connections for web workloads, take online backups, and know the limits that call for a server database.
concepts.why: SQLite can run real production services, if you set it up deliberately and know where its limits are.
concepts.body:
Many live services now run on SQLite. A solid starting setup for a web app on one server:

- `PRAGMA journal_mode = WAL` (once) and `PRAGMA synchronous = NORMAL`.
- `PRAGMA busy_timeout = 5000` and `PRAGMA foreign_keys = ON` on every connection.
- Write transactions with `BEGIN IMMEDIATE`, kept short. Many apps send all writes through **a single writer connection** (or a queue) and use a pool of read-only connections; this removes waiting for locks entirely.
- `PRAGMA optimize` from time to time; optionally `PRAGMA mmap_size` and a larger `cache_size` for read-heavy loads.
- Keep the database on a local disk (not a network drive), on the same machine as the app.

**Backups**: never just copy a live file. Use the **backup API** (`con.backup(target)` in Python, `.backup` in the sqlite3 tool) or `VACUUM INTO 'snapshot.db'`.

For continuous protection, a tool such as **Litestream** sends every change in the WAL to cloud file storage as it happens, so you can restore to a recent moment. Run `PRAGMA integrity_check` on restored copies.

**Limits**: one writer at a time (how many writes per second depends on transaction size and disk speed); no built-in network access, user accounts or replication; and one machine. When you need many writers across machines, automatic failover to a standby server, or fine-grained access control, move to a client-server database. Your SQL and schema knowledge transfers directly.
concepts.code:
import sqlite3, os, tempfile

def open_db(path, readonly=False):
    uri = f"file:{path}?mode={'ro' if readonly else 'rwc'}"
    con = sqlite3.connect(uri, uri=True, isolation_level=None, timeout=5)
    con.execute("PRAGMA foreign_keys = ON")
    con.execute("PRAGMA synchronous = NORMAL")
    return con

d = tempfile.mkdtemp()
writer = open_db(os.path.join(d, "app.db"))
writer.execute("PRAGMA journal_mode = WAL")
writer.execute("CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS event (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, kind TEXT)")
writer.execute("BEGIN IMMEDIATE")
writer.executemany("INSERT INTO event (kind) VALUES (?)", [("signup",), ("login",)])
writer.execute("COMMIT")

reader = open_db(os.path.join(d, "app.db"), readonly=True)
print(reader.execute("SELECT count(*) FROM event").fetchone())        # (2,)

backup = sqlite3.connect(os.path.join(d, "backup.db"))
writer.backup(backup)                         # consistent online copy
print(backup.execute("PRAGMA integrity_check").fetchone())            # ('ok',)
writer.execute(f"VACUUM INTO '{os.path.join(d, 'snapshot.db')}'")
takeaways: WAL + synchronous=NORMAL + busy timeout + short IMMEDIATE transactions
A single writer connection plus read-only readers avoids contention
Back up with the backup API, VACUUM INTO or Litestream, never a raw copy
pitfalls: Backing up with cp while the app is writing, producing a corrupt or inconsistent copy.

quiz.q: What is the safest way to back up a live SQLite database from Python?
options: Run DELETE FROM on a copy
quiz.explain: The backup API copies a consistent snapshot even while the database is in use.
